quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on stripes, checks, turned twills and the rules for putting weaves side by side.

questions.q: A stripe design changes the weave in which direction?
options: Across the picks only
Across the ends only
Across both ends and picks
Along the diagonal
questions.explain: A stripe runs warp-way: the weave changes as you move across the ends, but every pick is treated the same way. Changing across picks as well gives a check.

questions.q: What turns a stripe into a check?
options: Using two colours of yarn
Reversing the twill direction
Doubling the number of ends
Also changing the weave across the picks
questions.explain: A check changes the weave in both directions, so blocks of different weave appear across and along the cloth. Colour is not needed.

questions.q: Under what condition can two weaves be placed side by side without trouble?
options: When they have the same (or a common multiple) number of picks in the repeat and interlace with similar frequency
When they have the same number of ends in the repeat
When both are warp-faced
When they are woven from the same count of yarn
questions.explain: Side-by-side weaves must come back into step along the picks and must take up similarly, or the cloth puckers. Equal ends per repeat is not required for a stripe.

questions.q: What should happen at the join between two weaves in a stripe to give a clean cut?
options: Both weaves should show warp floats at the join
Both weaves should show weft floats at the join
Warp floats of one weave should meet weft floats of the other
The join should be covered by a plain-weave end
questions.explain: Opposite floats meeting at the join make a sharp line; like floats meeting run together and blur the boundary.

questions.q: Placing a loosely interlacing weave beside a tightly interlacing one is likely to make the cloth pucker.
questions.explain: Different interlacing frequency means different take-up and shrinkage in the two stripes, so one stripe cockles against the other.

questions.q: In a "turned twill" check, what is turned?
options: The cloth, which is woven face down
The direction of the twill line, reversed in adjacent blocks
The warp, which becomes the weft
The reed, to change the sett
questions.explain: The same twill is woven with the diagonal running Z in one block and S in the next, so the blocks differ only in twill direction.

questions.q: In the plain / 3-1 twill check, the twill squares look flatter and lighter than the plain squares.
questions.explain: The lecture says the opposite: plain squares look flat and light, twill squares dense and lustrous because of their longer floats.

questions.q: Why does the warp-face / weft-face combination show a check even in one colour of yarn?
options: Because the two squares use different counts of yarn
Because the squares are dyed after weaving
Because the twill direction alternates
Because squares of different structure reflect light differently
questions.explain: Plain squares alternate with squares where the ends work in groups (a rib-type weave); the contrast in surface, not in colour, makes the check visible.

questions.q: Which twill is turned in the lecture's 36-end check?
options: 3/3 twill
2/2 twill
2/1 twill
3/1 twill
questions.explain: The large example turns a 3/3 twill in blocks of 24 and 12 ends and picks on a 36 × 36 repeat.

questions.q: A check can be obtained from a stripe design simply by also changing the weave at intervals along the picks.
questions.explain: That is the definition: a stripe changes weave across the ends, a check across the picks as well.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Repeat sizes, common multiples and what changes when weaves are combined in stripes and checks.

questions.q: A stripe places 8 ends of 2/2 twill Z beside 8 ends of 2/2 twill S. How many ends are in the stripe repeat?
questions.explain: 8 + 8 = 16 ends, the lecture's stripe example.

questions.q: Plain weave (2 picks) is placed beside a 3/1 twill (4 picks) in a stripe. On how many picks must the stripe repeat?
questions.explain: The repeat is the lowest common multiple of 2 and 4, which is 4 picks; the plain weave simply repeats twice.

questions.q: Plain weave (2 picks) is placed beside a 2/1 twill (3 picks). On how many picks must the stripe repeat?
questions.explain: The lowest common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6 picks: three plain repeats beside two twill repeats.

questions.q: What happens when two weaves of very different interlacing frequency are placed side by side?
options: The twill line disappears
The cloth becomes heavier
The cloth puckers because the stripes take up differently
The join becomes sharper
questions.explain: Tight and loose stripes shrink by different amounts, so the cloth cockles; this is why the rules ask for similar interlacing frequency.

questions.q: In the 16 × 16 check in which the twill direction is turned in each quarter, how big is each quarter?
questions.explain: Four equal quarters of a 16 × 16 repeat are 8 ends × 8 picks each, holding two 2/2 twill repeats each way.

questions.q: In the 36-end check, blocks of 24 and 12 ends together make up the 36-end repeat.
questions.explain: 24 + 12 = 36 ends, and likewise 24 + 12 = 36 picks, giving the 36 × 36 repeat.

questions.q: Why should the block sizes in a turned 3/3 twill check be multiples of 6?
options: So that every block contains whole repeats of the 6-thread twill
So that the check is square
Because dobby looms only count in sixes
So that the blocks are all the same size
questions.explain: A 3/3 twill repeats on 6 ends and 6 picks; blocks of 24 and 12 hold 4 and 2 whole repeats, so the twill is not cut mid-repeat at the block edge.

questions.q: If the width of each stripe in the Z/S twill stripe is doubled, what happens to the repeat?
options: Ends and picks both double
Picks double, ends unchanged
Nothing changes
Ends double, picks unchanged
questions.explain: Stripe width is measured in ends, so the end repeat doubles (16 → 32); the pick repeat depends only on the twill and stays as it was.

questions.q: A check turns the twill in blocks of 24 and 12 ends and blocks of 24 and 12 picks. How many blocks does one repeat contain?
questions.explain: Two divisions across the ends × two along the picks = 4 blocks: 24 × 24, 24 × 12, 12 × 24 and 12 × 12.

questions.q: When a 2/2 twill is turned from Z to S at a stripe join, which of these changes?
options: The number of picks in the twill repeat
The direction of the twill diagonal
The float length
The proportion of warp and weft on the face
questions.explain: Turning the twill reverses the step direction only; the repeat, the 2-thread floats and the 50 : 50 face balance of a 2/2 twill stay the same.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting squares, blocks, repeats and hex digits in the lecture's stripe and check designs.

questions.q: The 36-end check repeats on 36 ends × 36 picks. How many point-paper squares does one repeat occupy?
questions.explain: 36 × 36 = 1,296 squares in one repeat.

questions.q: How many ends are in the repeat of a 3/3 twill?
questions.explain: A 3/3 twill has each end up for 3 picks and down for 3, so the repeat is 3 + 3 = 6 ends (and 6 picks).

questions.q: How many complete 3/3 twill repeats fit across a 24-end block?
questions.explain: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 whole twill repeats across the wide block.

questions.q: How many complete 3/3 twill repeats fit across the 12-end block?
questions.explain: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 whole twill repeats across the narrow block.

questions.q: The 36-end check is woven at 72 ends per inch. How many repeats are there per inch of width?
questions.explain: 72 ÷ 36 = 2 repeats per inch, so each 24-end block is one third of an inch wide.

questions.q: The 16 × 16 turned check is drawn at 2× repeat. How many ends are shown across the drawing?
questions.explain: Two repeats of 16 ends = 32 ends across.

questions.q: A stripe has 12 ends of plain weave beside 12 ends of 2/2 twill. How many ends are in the stripe repeat?
questions.explain: 12 + 12 = 24 ends in the repeat.

questions.q: For that same stripe (plain beside 2/2 twill), how many picks are in the repeat?
questions.explain: Plain repeats on 2 picks and 2/2 twill on 4; the lowest common multiple is 4 picks.

questions.q: The first pick of a 3/3 twill on 6 ends lifts ends 1, 2 and 3. With two padding zeros, what is the hex code of this pick?
questions.explain: 1 1 1 0 0 0 + 00 = 1110 0000 = $E0. $C0 (1100 0000) lifts only two ends and $07 lifts the last three bits instead of the first.

questions.q: One repeat of the 32 × 32 plain / 3-1 twill check contains 1,024 squares.
questions.explain: 32 × 32 = 1,024 squares, each either a plain-weave or a twill square according to its block.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing, drafting and troubleshooting stripe and check designs in the design office and on the loom.

questions.q: A stripe of plain weave beside a 5-end satin puckers badly. What is the reason?
options: The two weaves interlace with very different frequency, so the stripes take up differently
Satin cannot be woven beside any other weave
The stripe is too narrow
The satin was woven S instead of Z
questions.explain: Plain interlaces on every pick, satin only once in five; the plain stripe shrinks more and the cloth cockles. Satin has no twill direction to reverse.

questions.q: The boundary between two stripes looks ragged and blurred. What should the designer change?
options: Use a finer yarn
Increase the picks per inch
Rearrange the weaves so that warp floats of one meet weft floats of the other at the join
Add a third weave between them
questions.explain: A clean cut needs opposite floats meeting at the join; where like floats meet the two stripes merge.

questions.q: A mill wants a check in a single-colour yarn without buying coloured yarn. Which design meets the brief?
options: A hound's tooth
A warp-face / weft-face (plain beside rib-type) combination
A plain weave with a coloured weft
A printed check
questions.explain: Alternating plain squares with squares of a rib-type weave makes a check appear in one colour through the difference in surface; the other options need colour or printing.

questions.q: A turned 2/2 twill check needs two colours of yarn to be visible.
questions.explain: The reversal of the twill diagonal shows in one colour because the floats catch the light in opposite directions.

questions.q: To weave the 36-end turned 3/3 twill check, what is the minimum number of healds with a straight draft for each block?
questions.explain: Each block of ends needs its own six healds for the 3/3 twill because the two blocks lift differently; 6 + 6 = 12 healds on a dobby.

questions.q: Which pair of weaves can go side by side in a stripe with least risk of puckering?
options: 2/2 twill Z and 2/2 twill S
Plain and 8-end satin
Plain and 4/4 twill
5-end sateen and 1/7 twill
questions.explain: The two 2/2 twills are the same weave in opposite directions, so their interlacing frequency is identical; the other pairs mix tight and very loose weaves.

questions.q: A plain / 3-1 twill check sample in a dull cotton shows only a faint check. What would make it clearer?
options: Reduce the twill blocks to 2 × 2 squares
Change the twill to plain
Use a more lustrous yarn, because the effect depends on light reflected from the twill floats
Weave the cloth face down
questions.explain: The contrast is between flat plain squares and lustrous twill squares, so yarn lustre (for example mercerised cotton) strengthens the effect.

questions.q: A 16-end stripe of 2/2 twill Z beside 2/2 twill S can be woven on 8 healds, four for each stripe.
questions.explain: Each 2/2 twill needs four healds; the two stripes lift in different orders, so they need their own sets: 4 + 4 = 8.

questions.q: A stripe is already on the loom and the designer wants to turn it into a check without re-drawing the warp. What must be changed?
options: The draft
The peg plan (lifting plan)
The reed
The warp colour order
questions.explain: A check changes the weave across the picks, which is controlled entirely by the lifting order; the draft and reed stay as they are.

questions.q: A customer asks for weft-way bands (stripes across the cloth) of plain and 2/2 twill. How is this produced?
options: By changing the draft every few ends
By changing the reed count
By using two warp beams
By changing the weave at intervals along the picks through the lifting plan
questions.explain: Bands across the cloth are a change of weave along the picks, which the peg plan controls; the warp is threaded uniformly.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions on repeat arithmetic, block sizes and the reasoning behind the combining rules.

questions.q: How does a herringbone differ from a turned-twill check?
options: Herringbone uses a different twill angle
Herringbone needs two colours
Herringbone turns the twill across the ends only (a stripe), the check turns it across the picks as well
There is no difference
questions.explain: Herringbone is the stripe form of a turned twill; add the reversal along the picks and the same idea becomes a check.

questions.q: A stripe combines plain weave (2 picks), 2/2 twill (4 picks) and 2/1 twill (3 picks) side by side. On how many picks must it repeat?
questions.explain: The lowest common multiple of 2, 4 and 3 is 12 picks (6 plain, 3 of 2/2 twill and 4 of 2/1 twill repeats).

questions.q: Why did the lecture choose blocks of 24 and 12 ends rather than, say, 20 and 16 for the 3/3 twill check?
options: Because 24 and 12 are multiples of the 6-end twill repeat and 20 and 16 are not
Because the check must be in the ratio 2 : 1
Because 36 is the largest repeat a dobby allows
Because 20 + 16 is not 36
questions.explain: Blocks must hold whole twill repeats; 20 ÷ 6 and 16 ÷ 6 are not whole numbers, so the twill would be cut mid-repeat at the block edge.

questions.q: A check made by turning one twill has the same number of interlacings in every block, so it does not pucker.
questions.explain: The weave is identical in all blocks, only its direction differs, so take-up is uniform; the combining rule is automatically satisfied.

questions.q: The 36-end check is woven at 90 ends per inch on a 60-inch wide warp. How many repeats fit across the width?
questions.explain: Total ends = 90 × 60 = 5,400; 5,400 ÷ 36 = 150 repeats across.

questions.q: A student places a 3/1 twill beside a 1/3 twill in a stripe. What should be expected?
options: Puckering, because the weaves have different pick repeats
A sound stripe: both repeat on 4 picks with equal interlacing, and the warp-faced stripe contrasts with the weft-faced one
No visible stripe, because both are the same twill
A ragged join, because twill cannot meet twill
questions.explain: 3/1 and 1/3 twills are the same weave seen from opposite faces, so they interlace equally and come back into step every 4 picks, while their faces look different.

questions.q: A designer insists on plain weave beside 2/2 twill in a stripe. What precaution reduces the risk of puckering?
options: Make the twill S instead of Z
Add a satin stripe between them
Double the picks per inch
Give the plain stripe a slightly lower sett or finer yarn so its take-up is closer to the twill's
questions.explain: Plain interlaces twice as often as 2/2 twill; easing the plain stripe's density brings the take-up of the two stripes closer. Twill direction has no effect on take-up.

questions.q: The warp-face / weft-face combination repeats on 20 ends. At 80 ends per inch, what is the width of one repeat in inches?
questions.explain: 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25 inch, so four repeats fit in each inch.

questions.q: In a stripe of 2/2 twill Z beside 2/2 twill S, the twill lines meet at the join to form a V-shaped (herringbone-like) line.
questions.explain: The diagonals run in opposite directions in adjacent stripes, so they meet at the join in a chevron, which is exactly the herringbone appearance.

questions.q: In the 16 × 16 turned check each quarter is 8 × 8 of 2/2 twill. How many complete 2/2 twill repeats does one quarter contain?
questions.explain: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 repeats across and 2 along, so 2 × 2 = 4 repeats per quarter.
